Of this mantra of the *Śrī Mahāmāryāṣṭaka-stotra*, Vararuci is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*), the illustrious Mahāmārī, the Great Power, is the deity (*devatā*), Oṃ Kālī is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Oṃ Mahākālī is the power (*śakti*), and Oṃ Bhadrakālī is the pin (*kīlaka*) for my [protection from] Mahāmārī.

The application (*viniyoga*) is that one should recite [this mantra] for the purpose of dispelling all fears, ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, *ḍākinīs*, and *śākinīs*, as well as for the attainment of my desired objects and aims.
Thus, with palms joined in reverence: *Oṃ*, salutation to the seer Vararuci; [place this] on the head. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre.

The application [of this mantra] is for the purpose of reciting it with the desire to pacify great pestilence, fear, ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, *ḍākinīs*, *śākinīs*, and all calamities, and for the sake of attaining the supreme, desired, and cherished accomplishment.

6a) [He stands] holding the great horn of Yama’s buffalo in his hand, filled with the feathers of Tārkṣya and the blood-red remnants of corpses.

Having fashioned her own foot-ornament from a single iron chain, with a single braid left hanging down and a wretched brass earring,
she wanders this world like a female elephant whose ears are bound by a tethered rope smeared with poison, appearing like a withered ear-ornament.
O Goddess, whose outstretched arms are like an increasing banner and canopy, be gracious!

O Goddess of the World, at the terrible moment when the end of saṃsāra arrives, the entire universe enters into Your mouth with its fangs, drenched in the blood and fat of men, amidst the smoke and rising clouds of the universal conflagration.
You are Kālī, the bearer of skulls, reclining upon a corpse; You are the Yoginī of the Yoga-mudrā, whose face is both straight and curved.
O Śivā Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, may you remove the fear of death from Mārī.
Having made a garland of the heads of enemies severed with your beautiful teeth in battle, you danced while increasing that wreath; then, having entered the cremation ground,
you were seen by many spirits as you wore a girdle of great lordly elephants bound tightly around your broad hips.
At night, their hands were occupied with roots and swords, and their eyes were copper-red from intoxication with the honey of blood.
In this [battle], where the Pramathas have severed the heads with their knives, there are vessels for drinking blood;
(in another reading: *prāṇasṛkpātrāṇi*) there are cloths wrapped around the buttocks, and there are faces fashioned from the stalks of the Sādhyas' lotuses, with bells ringing upon raised staffs.

May Kāpālinī protect me—she whose lips are ever turned toward [the offering], who carries away the praises of the Vaśā, who is worshipped with offerings, and who, with a snap of her teeth, devours the flesh of the dead. 10.

May Bhadrakālī protect us— she who, having drawn her lute from the very depths of Pātāla with the beauty of its strings vibrating through rhythmic performance, plays it upon the head of a ram whose feet wander like knotted masses of flesh and whose neck is bowed; she who strikes it with the tips of the great horns of a buffalo.
The lute of Brahma’s skull is pervaded by the dissolution of the world.

Cāmuṇḍā, who has donned a garment of human skin after instantly devouring the world along with the gods and asuras; whose half-bound topknot is entwined with serpents and adorned with the heads of corpses strung upon a thread like a garland of hungry ghosts, and who is impaled upon a thread spread out by the terrifying, blazing flames of the fire of universal transmigration.
May Caṇḍamuṇḍī, who is anointing her head which has been crushed and churned, purify [us]. || 12 ||

Beholding Bhadrā, Raudrī, Manīyā, and Manapiṣitamukhī, who are full in the left [breasts], the ten Mothers, with their faces bowed, immediately pay homage to you. May the stainless-limbed one, whose course is white and so forth, [grant] the removal of impurity day after day.

May she, whose feet serve as a vessel for the water of the eyes of every living being, destroy the very limits of the path of destruction. 13.
Chewing upon a fragment of bone, making a fierce and tumultuous *kaṭakaṭa* sound,
that emaciated woman laughs a terrible laugh of "ka ha ka ha" amidst the assembly of pretas.

May this Caṇḍī protect us— she who is eternally intent on dance, who sounds the *ḍamaru*, *ḍimiḍima*, and *ḍiṇḍima* drums, who makes the *jha-jha-ma-jhama-jhamā-jhaṃ-pamā* sounds, and who consumes all with her roar.
By her, death perishes, even minor sins flee, misfortunes do not approach, and enemies are destroyed.

Diseases, other afflictions following the dissolution [of the world], seizing spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, venomous serpents, scorpions, fire, thieves, and assassins— none of these exist for him who recites this hymn to the Goddess composed by Vararuci. (15)
Those who, with devotion and single-minded focus on her, recite here at the time of the twilight junction this hymn to the noble Lady Māryā— which burns away misfortune and was composed by Vararuci—
will have their poverty, diseases, and fear of blazing fires swiftly destroyed by the Mother of the World within this saṃsāra.
May Bhadrakālī, the bestower of auspiciousness, who roars with a terrible sound, take away my fear. || 16 ||
It removes the fear of pestilence, smallpox, and epidemics; it dispels the threat of *vetālas* and spirits;

it neutralizes the poison of thieves, tigers, great serpents, and the like; it quells cold fevers and burning pains; it bestows fortune upon women, brings compassion, purifies one's character, and grants excellent sons.
One should recite this hymn, which bestows desired fruits, consisting of the mantra of the eight Māris, at the three junctions of the day.
Thus ends the Mahāmāryāṣṭaka composed by Vararuci, within the Kālīkhaṇḍa of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. May there be auspiciousness!

Kārttikeya said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O cause of creation, preservation, and destruction!
You are the refuge of all the gods; you are the refuge of all embodied beings;
you alone are indeed the refuge of all deities and the destitute alike.
You alone are the support of the world; you alone are the cause of the universe.
You alone are the one to be worshipped by all; apart from you, I have no other refuge.
What is the supreme secret in this world? And what is the ultimate goal?
What is the one supreme excellence? What is the yoga that grants liberation from everything—without pilgrimage, without austerity, without gifts, and without sacrifices?
By what kind of meditation without dissolution could one attain perfection?
From what does creation arise, and in what does dissolution occur?
"By what means, O Lord, is one crossed over from the perilous ocean of saṃsāra?
I wish to hear that; please tell me, O Maheśvara."
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Excellent, O Pārvatī! You have asked me well concerning my son Nandana. There is a most secret matter; I shall tell it to you, my son, without any doubt.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others;
and whatever other fierce beings there were, they too were previously born from primordial nature (prakṛti).
She alone is the Goddess, the Great Power, Śyāmā, Dakṣiṇakālikā;
she alone gives birth to the universe, and she alone is protected by you.
She alone withdraws this entire universe, with all its moving and unmoving beings;
she is the support of all creatures and the remover of the affliction of disease.
The power of will, as well as knowledge, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
exists in a threefold form as Śakti, effecting creation, maintenance, and destruction.
In the form of Brahmā he creates, in the form of Viṣṇu he protects,
and in the form of Rudra he destroys this entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
In that womb the entire world, including its waste, proceeds;
in it all is dissolved at the end, and from it it is born again.
Having propitiated her, the supreme state was attained throughout the three worlds;
I shall now recite her thousand names, so listen.

shall attain omniscience, O Goddess, through the grace of Siddhikālī.

Kālarudra is the agent of dissolution, and Īśvara is eternally the agent of absorption; what need is there for much speaking here? That Goddess [is attained] by mere meditation.
Liberation occurs even while one is still alive; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
